questions.stem: Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of Myelodysplastic syndrome?
questions.solutionHtml:
Leucoerythroblastic blood picture
  • Myelodysplastic syndrome usually results in pancytopenia rather than leukoerythroblastic blood picture.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 620, 621

All of the above
  • Pseudo-Pelger-Hüet neutrophils: bilobed hypo-granular dysplastic neutrophils seen in Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), Accelerated phase of CML, AML with dysplastic maturation.
  • Pseudo-Pelger-Hüet cells, neutrophils with only two nuclear lobes instead of the normal three to four, are observed at the top and bottom of this field.



Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 620, 621

questions.stem: In myelodysplastic syndrome, ring sideroblast is seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Mitochondria
  • In myelodysplastic syndrome, ring sideroblast is seen in Mitochondria
  • Within the erythroid series, common abnormalities include ring sideroblasts and erythroblasts with iron-laden mitochondria visible as perinuclear granules in Prussian blue–stained aspirates or biopsies.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 620, 621

questions.stem: Which of the following is not compatible with a diagnosis of juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia -

options.label: B
options.text: Increased haemoglobin F levels for age

options.label: D
options.text: GM-CSF hypersensitivity of myeloid progenitors in vitro

questions.solutionHtml:
Presence of BCR-ABL fusion gene
  • The presence of BCR-ABL fusion gene is not compatible with a diagnosis of juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia (JMML)
  • The Philadelphia chromosome is seen in CML & some cases of ALL.


Wintrobe's Clinical Hematology, 12th Edition, Page No. 2001, Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20th Edition Page No. 788, 789

questions.stem: Which is the most common cytogenetic abnormality in adult myelodysplastic syndrome(MDS) -
questions.solutionHtml:
5q-
  • The cytogenetic anomalies in MDS include deletion (5q), most common -7, +8, -5 and -18 as the most frequent changes, in the order shown.


Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page No. 620, 621
